svg.aria-label: Diagram: DynamoDB bulk put items loads data from Amazon S3 into an existing table on a write path that AWS says consumes none of the table's read or write capacity, which distinguishes it from Import from Amazon S3 that creates a new table. The capacity claim is precisely scoped, and four other things connected to the table still behave differently. DynamoDB Streams and Kinesis data streams receive a record for every bulk write delivered at the operation's write rate, so consumers sized for normal traffic can fall behind and a consumer more than 24 hours behind loses records; MaxWriteRequestUnits caps the operation's rate, with a minimum of 1,024. Bulk writes do not appear in the table's ConsumedWriteCapacityUnits metric or in Contributor Insights because they consume no capacity. Bulk writes bypass DAX, so cached items stay stale until their DAX TTL expires. CloudTrail logs the StartBulkOperation call but not individual item writes. The diagram also records that with no condition expression an item is written unconditionally and overwrites any existing item with the same key, that DynamoDB can write some records a second time after an internal failover so a version guard is needed, that cancelling does not roll back items already written, that global tables are not supported, and the quotas of 100 GB Standard and 1 TB Accelerated input per operation with one active operation per table.
svg.title: No capacity consumed is not the same as no impact
svg.text: The claim is precisely scoped. Four other things still feel the write.
“The writes run on a separate path and consume none of the table’s read or write capacity.”
What it is, and what it is not
“Import from Amazon S3 creates a new table … bulk put items writes into a table that already exists.”
Connected to your table — and what a bulk write does to each
table capacity nothing. This is the whole of the claim.
Streams / Kinesis a record per write, “at the operation’s write rate”
metrics absent from ConsumedWriteCapacityUnits and Contributor Insights
DAX bypassed; cached items “stay stale until their DAX TTL expires”
CloudTrail the start call only; “Individual item writes are not logged”
Invisible to the metric you would watch; highly visible to the consumer least able to absorb it.
The stream is where it hurts, and the penalty is not latency
“Consumers sized for normal traffic can fall behind. DynamoDB Streams retains records for 24 hours, so a
consumer more than 24 hours behind loses records.”
Cap it with MaxWriteRequestUnits (minimum 1,024) — throttling the thing whose point was not throttling.
Safety is per item, and opt-in
“When no condition expression is specified … the item
is written unconditionally, overwriting any existing
item with the same key.”
Which matters because of this
“DynamoDB can write some records a second time
after an internal failover.” Carry a version attribute
and guard on it.
Also: no global tables, no rollback on cancel, one active operation per table.
100 GB input per operation on Standard, 1 TB on Accelerated, 50,000 objects, 5 GB each. Cancelling stops
future writes only — “DynamoDB does not roll back items that were written before the cancellation”.
One API call can rewrite a hundred gigabytes and leave one CloudTrail event.
